definition: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a process where a computer constructs or updates a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously keeping track of an entity's location within it.
details: While this initially appears to be a chicken or the egg problem, there are several algorithms known to solve it in, at least approximately, tractable time for certain environments. Popular approximate solution methods include the particle filter, extended Kalman filter, covariance intersection, and GraphSLAM. SLAM algorithms are based on concepts in computational geometry and computer vision, and are used in robot navigation, robotic mapping and odometry for virtual reality or augmented reality. SLAM algorithms are tailored to the available resources and are not aimed at perfection but at operational compliance. Published approaches are employed in self-driving cars, unmanned aerial vehicles, autonomous underwater vehicles, planetary rovers, newer domestic robots and even inside the human body.

explainer.lead: SLAM lets a computer build a map of an unknown place while tracking where it is in that map at the same time. It is what lets robots and AR systems navigate without a pre-made map.

tiers.eli5: Like walking through a dark maze with a torch, drawing the walls as you go and working out where you stand on your own drawing.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers choose filters or graph-based methods depending on the environment and sensor set, fusing lidar, camera or odometry data. A pitfall is drift, where small errors accumulate until the map and pose diverge.
tiers.paperLevel: Common approximate methods include the particle filter, extended Kalman filter, covariance intersection and GraphSLAM; tractability holds for certain environments, not in general.

explainer.example: A robot vacuum enters a new room, builds a map from its sensor readings and locates itself within that map as it cleans.
